Learning Objectives
Define patient-reported outcomes and patient-reported outcome measures and how they
differ from traditional outcome metrics.
Review the types of patient-reported outcome measures.
Discuss the manner in which patient-reported outcome measures can be administered and
collected.
Specify how patient-reported outcome measures can be used to strengthen research and
support or guide clinical decision making.
Recognize the current challenges in collecting and using patient-reported outcome measures
in routine musculoskeletal care.

Important Definitions and Context
A patient-reported outcome (PRO) is defined as “any report of the status of a patient’s health
condition that comes directly from the patient, without interpretation of the patient’s response
by a clinician or anyone else.”1
Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) are the tools or instruments (typically validated
questionnaires) designed to captures PROs.
PROs differ from prior information gathered and assessed to help measure healthcare quality,
such as claim-based outcomes (eg, discharge destination) or process metrics (eg, time to
antibiotic agents for an open fracture or completion of a perioperative safety checklist). As
health care transitions to reward value, measuring factors most important to patients (ie,
PROs) will be imperative.

Important Definitions and Context
Although many individuals interchange PROs and PROMs, a subtle, yet important,
difference exists between them that should be acknowledged. PROs provide insight from
a patient’s point of view. This insight is directly from the patient and is not interpreted by
a physician or other stakeholder.2 Such information empowers patients and allows them
to be more active participants in their own care. A more robust and systematic method
for measuring PROs are PROMs. To better understand the nuanced difference between
PROs and PROMs, consider the following simple example. If a patient states, “My pain is
well controlled,” this may be considered a PRO. If a patient uses the 0 to 10 numeric pain
rating scale and reports that his or her pain is a 3 out of 10, this would be considered a
PROM to quantify the PRO of pain. Not all PROMs are of the same quality.
The growing importance of assessing PROs via routine PROM collection is crucial as
healthcare systems continue transitioning away from rewarding quantity via fee-for-
service payment mechanisms and toward rewarding quality via a value-based healthcare
approach. Specifically, PROMs provide an assessment of quality by measuring clinical
outcomes most important to the patient. Historically, claims-based outcomes (eg,
discharge destination) or process measures (eg, time to antibiotic agents for an open
fracture or completion of a perioperative safety checklist) have been used as measures
of healthcare quality. Although such information can provide important insight and may

9/3/26, 5:34 PM
AAOS | Patient-Reported Outcome Measures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004014
2/19

play a key role in assessing care efficiency and general patient safety, an evaluation of
patient-centered clinical outcomes is missing. Moving forward, PROs must be collected
using validated PROMs in a routine manner, similar to claims-based outcomes and
process measures.
Background
PROMs were initially developed for research, specifically within the health services and
pharmacologic arenas.3,4
The use of PROMs can empower patients and ease the evaluation and sharing of each
patient’s health status among physicians.5,6
PROMs allow for assessment of the outcomes most important to patients to be readily
quantified—in real time—as part of routine clinical care.6,7

Background
PROMs provide an avenue for patients to have a greater voice in their own clinical care.8
The routine collection and discussion of PROMs is necessary to begin to appreciate their
full potential and value. Although an explosion in the interest and use of PROMs across
orthopaedic surgery has occurred, a great deal of work remains to make PROMs
common in all clinics and hospital settings in a manner that allows for the scores to be
used practically.9
Requirements of an Optimal PROM
The best PROMs are valid, reliable, and responsive to change; have low ceiling and/or floor
effects; can be efficiently and easily completed by patients; and have scores that are easily
understood by clinicians.
PROMs should be standardized across a practice as much as possible. In the short term, this
facilitates data aggregation and comparison for research and quality improvement initiatives.

9/3/26, 5:34 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004014
3/19

In the long term, this may facilitate easier reporting of PROMs if they become required by
payors.

Requirements of an Optimal PROM
A wide variety of PROMs are available for use in orthopaedic care. Surgeons must
understand key characteristics of an optimal PROM.
First, the construct being targeted for evaluation must actually be evaluated. For
example, if your PROM attempts to measure physical function, surgeons must ensure
that it truly measures physical function. This concept is called validity.10
Second, high-quality PROMs allow for consistent scores that enable differentiation
between stable patients despite measurement errors on repeat administration. This
concept is called reliability.10
Third, as patients improve or worsen, PROMs should be able to easily capture this
change. This concept is called responsiveness.10
Fourth, at the extremes of a symptom state, surgeons must appreciate differences
among patients. Therefore, acceptable ceiling and floor effects, defined as the
proportion of patients completing a PROM scoring the highest (ceiling) or lowest (floor)
possible score, are necessary.11 For example, PROMs in which 50% of patients
demonstrate the same excellent physical function score across a population likely do not
differentiate between small, yet important, differences among patients.
Fifth, being able to collect PROMs in an efficient and timely manner should be a focus of
stakeholders in selecting and using PROMs in daily clinical practice.12 Streamlining the
collection of PROMs reduces responder burden, likely increasing the number of patients
who are willing to complete PROMs.13

Lastly, PROMs that provide easy-to-understand and actionable scores measured across
the care cycle are ideal. Indeed, repeated collection of PROMs over time with ongoing
management allows for real-time evaluation of care and may help guide clinical
decisions if the scores are easily comprehensible and surgeons are well versed in the
instruments.14 Although this may sound straightforward, a great deal of work is
necessary to determine how best to visualize and take action on PROM data.9
Understanding PROMs in Orthopaedic Surgery
PROMs can be general (eg, specific to overall functional or health status), anatomic-specific (eg,
specific to the hand), or disease-specific (eg, specific to knee osteoarthritis).

Understanding PROMs in Orthopaedic Surgery
A wide variety of PROMs are available for use in orthopaedic surgery research and
clinical care. For example, even within total joint arthroplasty, a recent evaluation of the
literature revealed 42 unique PROMs used across 644 studies in four major orthopaedic
surgery journals.15 Extrapolating this finding across orthopaedic subspecialties and the
wide range of conditions and procedures possible, the number of possible PROMs is
extremely high. Importantly, among the numerous PROMs possible, general and
condition-specific instruments may be used.
General PROMs focus on a construct in the setting of any orthopaedic condition. For
example, to gain an overarching understanding of a patient’s general health status, the
Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) Global-10 Form
offers invaluable insight.16 In addition, the PROMIS Physical Function17 or Upper
Extremity18 domain are useful in providing general functional status insight without
being too anatomically or disease focused. The PROMIS Physical Function or Upper
Extremity domain are not the only general functional PROMs, and a number of possible
general PROMs can be used across many different constructs (eg, quality of life, pain, or
mental health).19 The value of general PROMs is that they can be used in the setting of
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:34 PM
AAOS | Patient-Reported Outcome Measures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004014
5/19

any condition to assess the construct of interest. This may be of notable importance in
population health initiatives.
If a more localized PROM that is not disease-specific is desired, surgeons also can use
more focal anatomic-specific PROMs. An example of this type of PROM is the Michigan
Hand Questionnaire;20 however, more general PROMs are similarly responsive and
concurrently valid with the Michigan Hand Questionnaire.21 This finding is common in
the orthopaedic literature. Therefore, although more anatomic-specific PROMs are
available, the use of more general PROMs in clinical care and research is acceptable in
most situations.
In addition to general and anatomic-specific PROMs, condition-specific PROMs exist.
These instruments capture the effect of a disease on a patient’s self-reported health.
Examples of condition-specific PROMs include the Boston Carpal Tunnel Questionnaire22
and the Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score.23 Although commonly used in
appropriate patient populations, these PROMs are limited in scope to the specific
conditions being evaluated. In addition, similar to anatomic-specific PROMs, condition-
specific PROMs and general PROMs tend to perform similarly.21
Collection of PROMs
PROMs can be collected electronically or via a pen and paper; however, electronic collection
allows for simpler integration into electronic health records.
More recently developed PROMs are smart because they use item response theory (IRT) and
computerized adaptive testing (CAT).
PROMIS is a set of PROMs developed with support from the National Institutes of Health24 and
is growing in popularity within orthopaedic surgery.

Collection of PROMs
PROMs can be collected electronically on a computer, tablet (eg, iPad), or other
electronic device or via a pen and paper. Regardless of the collection method, research
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:34 PM
AAOS | Patient-Reported Outcome Measures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004014
6/19

has demonstrated that PROMs scores are equivalent;25-27 however, the ease of PROM
distribution and collection should be considered in selecting the most beneficial
approach. With the advancement of electronic health records, PROMs collected
electronically may be optimal because it also allows for easier data visualization and data
access for clinical research and care. In addition, because patients speak various
languages, collecting PROMs electronically can enable surgeons and their clinic staff to
more easily distribute PROMs in the language preferred by each patient. Although not all
PROMs have been translated into various languages, many of the more popular PROMs
are available in various languages. For example, PROMIS questionnaires are available in
many languages (eg, Spanish, German, French, Dutch, Korean, traditional Chinese, and
Hebrew, among others), and work is being performed to continue to translate the
questionnaire into even more languages.28 In addition, the literature suggests that
patients generally prefer electronic PROMs collection,29 and web-based technology and
patient computer literacy are improving.30 Importantly, irrespective of the distribution
and collection method, value can be derived by practicing orthopaedic surgeons as long
as validated PROMs are used.
An additional value of electronic PROMs collection is the ability to collect PROMs that use
IRT and CAT. As Brodke et al31 stated, “IRT is a contemporary process used to develop
tests that differentiate respondents along the continuum of a specific trait, such as
degrees of pain or levels of physical function.”32 In addition, the CAT approach allows for
only the necessary, minimum number of questions to be asked to evaluate a patient’s
condition fully; by doing so, the patient burden is minimized.31,32 The time to completion
is substantially shorter with PROMs that use IRT as part of a CAT than with legacy, static
PROMs.33,34 These elements of smart PROMs remove the static nature of legacy pen-
and-paper PROMs, which take additional time without providing greater insight in many
instances.
The PROMIS is one set of PROMs increasing in popularity within orthopaedic surgery.
Although static and smart versions of PROMIS questionnaires are available, the smart
variety that uses IRT as part of a CAT is of interest to many orthopaedic surgeons and
researchers. A growing call exists to make PROMIS CATs a routinely collected PROM in
musculoskeletal care35 because the questionnaire performs as well as, if not better than,
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:34 PM
AAOS | Patient-Reported Outcome Measures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004014
7/19

many legacy instruments.36 As PROM collection continues to weave its way into routine
orthopaedic care, stakeholders across clinics, hospitals, and health systems will need to
have a seat at the table to determine which PROMs—whether PROMIS CATs or static
legacy instruments—are collected and easily accessible to help guide shared clinical
decision making and improve research and policy work.
For PROMs to be widely collected, certain barriers must be overcome. These issues
include workflow concerns, financial and personnel considerations, and information
technology/security challenges, among others. To overcome these challenges, PROM
implementation and use experts have suggested a team-based approach with a PROM
physician champion leading the endeavor.37-39 In addition, standardizing which PROMs
are used, incorporating PROM completion into the baseline clinic flow, and investing in
additional paid support (eg, full-time equivalent individual) to ensure operational
oversight and quality control may be helpful.40 In addition, collaborating with
information technology professionals may ease collection and integration with electronic
health records if electronic PROMs are used and ensure the security of patient
information. Lastly, PROMs used should be written at or below a sixth- to eighth-grade
reading level based on the recommendation of the US National Institutes of Health and
the American Medical Association. Many PROMs—including PROMIS—fall within this
reading level range;41 however, patients who cannot complete PROMs because of their
age (eg, young pediatric orthopaedic patients) or mental status, whether a health
condition or otherwise, will always exist. For children, proxy instruments are available for
parents or guardians to complete.42 Unfortunately, no proxy instruments are available
for adult patients with intellectual disability or altered mental status; however, future
work may lead to these being developed. The reading level of and access to appropriate
PROMs for all patients should be monitored closely as they become more common in
routine clinical care. Although challenges exist in the routine collection of PROMs, these
strategies and areas for additional development can help solve key issues. Leaders must
be willing to be agile and adapt as improved strategies and solutions are determined.
Benefits of PROMs in Clinical Care and Research
Determine Who May Benefit From Surgical Treatment

9/3/26, 5:34 PM
AAOS | Patient-Reported Outcome Measures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004014
8/19

The minimal clinically important difference (MCID), or the change in a given PROM score that
represents the first clinically appreciable difference in patient symptom states (good or bad),
may help orthopaedic surgeons better understand which patients may benefit from surgical
treatment.
Ongoing research is being performed to better appreciate determine the change in a PROM
score that represents more than just the minimal clinical improvement, such as the substantial
clinical benefit.

Determine Who May Benefit From Surgical Treatment
Although PROMs are valuable tools at baseline to measure outcomes most important to
patients, they may be of greater value in assessing the well-being of a patient over time.
Determining the change in a PROM score from one point to another that represents
appreciable clinical improvement or worsening allows orthopaedic surgeons to monitor
each patient’s health status. Recognition that statistically significant changes in PROM
scores from one point to another may not be clinically significant is crucial.43 Therefore,
MCID, or the change in PROM score from one point to another, represents a true
clinically appreciable change in symptoms. After an appropriate MCID estimate is
understood, it can be used to assess patient health status over time using PROMs.
MCID estimates for a given PROM and condition or procedure can be determined via
several methods, two of the most common of which are discussed in this lesson. The
first approach is a distribution-based approach, which is a statistical method in which the
MCID estimate is one-half of one standard deviation of a given PROM.44 The second
approach is the anchor-based method, which evaluates the change in a given PROM in
relation to another question or patient factor, such as patient satisfaction or patient
acceptable symptom state, which asks the patient, “Based on your current level of
symptoms, do you feel your condition is satisfactory?”45,46 Because of the increasing
aspiration to use PROMs as a part of care delivery, interest in better understanding MCID
estimates for PROMs in upper extremity47 and lower extremity48 conditions has been
increasing.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:34 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004014
9/19

Despite the need for continued fine-tuning of MCID estimates and their use in routine
clinical care, many have already begun to assess those who may or may not benefit from
surgical treatment using PROMs in the orthopaedic surgery literature. These preliminary
evaluations have been completed for hand,49 shoulder,50 spine,51,52 hip and knee,53,54
foot and ankle,55,56 and sports conditions;57 however, work is ongoing to move beyond
understanding who may benefit minimally from a clinical standpoint to understanding
who may benefit substantially.58 As the power of PROMs to understand who may benefit
from surgical treatment increases, PROMs likely will become a more integral part of
clinical orthopaedic care.
Measure and Evaluate Outcomes Most Important to Patients
PROMs capture the outcomes most important to most patients receiving orthopaedic care,
such as quality of life, functional status, and pain, whereas traditional outcomes that are
measured do not.

Measure and Evaluate Outcomes Most Important to Patients
The term quality in health care, including within orthopaedic surgery, is vague and
without a clear definition.59 In addition, if metrics, such as those provided by the Centers
for Medicare & Medicaid Services are present, they tend not to be the core outcomes, or
at least the comprehensive patient-centered outcomes, sought by patients
preoperatively. For example, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Hospital
Compare tool provides a generic rate of complications by hospital for patients
undergoing total hip and knee arthroplasty;60 however, many patients seek hip or knee
arthroplasty to increase their functional status, decrease their pain, and improve their
quality of life rather than to avoid a complication. Although avoiding complications is
important, it is not the goal of patients seeking surgical management for hip or knee
osteoarthritis. Such data on functional status, pain, and quality of life are not
transparently shared nor readily accessible to the public by individual surgeons or by
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:34 PM
AAOS | Patient-Reported Outcome Measures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004014
10/19

hospitals and health systems; however, they are crucial and must be assessed via
PROMs.
Challenges Limiting Widespread Adoption and Use of PROMs in
Musculoskeletal Care
Barriers to Increasing PROM Buy-In
Routine collection of PROMs may be costly and requires a great deal of resources to
implement effectively.
Although PROMs have been increasing in popularity across orthopaedic surgery, their day-to-
day use in clinical care remains limited.
A great deal of potential exists for PROMs in daily musculoskeletal care, especially if healthcare
systems continue to transition away from volume and toward value, which is defined as health
outcomes achieved per dollar spent.61

Barriers to Increasing PROM Buy-In
Currently, although many orthopaedic surgeons incorporate PROMs into their practice,
many do not use PROMs in their care algorithms. This is despite the shift toward
rewarding healthcare value and the preliminary evidence that the use of PROMs
improves the patient experience in orthopaedic surgery.62 Clinicians may not value
PROMs in their clinical practice because of a few core reasons, including “failure to
generate actionable data, implementation obstacles, and inappropriate use of PROMs as
a performance metric, with concerns regarding inadequate risk adjustment.”63 As
greater insights are made to expand the manner in which PROM data are used in
practice and as large health systems continue their implementation of PROMs systems,
databases, and tools,7,64 the use of PROMs likely will mature within orthopaedic surgery.
The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons and the American Board of
Orthopaedic Surgery appear poised to take advantage of the power of PROMs and be
leaders across health care with their use. Indeed, the American Academy of Orthopaedic

11/19

Surgeons website, at the suggestion of the Quality Outcomes Data Work Group, includes
a recommended list of PROMs, which was approved in 2016.65 Although PROMs have
advanced since then, the commitment of the American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons to provide resources for this work over the years suggests it is an area of
focus. In addition, the American Board of Orthopaedic Surgery currently incorporates
PROMs, specifically PROMIS Physical Function and Pain Interference, in the certification
and recertification processes.66 Despite the progress made by these initiatives, barriers
remain to the widespread adoption and use of PROMs. Although the future of PROMs in
orthopaedic surgery remains to be seen, these initial steps taken by prestigious bodies
in the field of orthopaedic surgery demonstrate the commitment of orthopaedic surgery
leaders to incorporate PROMs robustly into education, research, and patient care in the
future.
